title: Mole fraction of B in the vapour phase in equilibrium with an ideal solution
summary: Type the stem's data into a dark equilibrium bench and run it through five stages: weigh out a kilogram of A and add B by molality, build the liquid mole fraction from the molecules on screen, let the vessel reach equilibrium and split the pressure gauge into p(A) and p(B) by Raoult's law, then put twenty-five molecules of each phase side by side and count - five are B in the liquid and only four in the vapour, which is the whole question.
subject: Chemistry
topic: Vapour-phase composition over an ideal solution
subtopics: Molality to mole fraction, and why the solvent's molar mass is needed
Raoult's law for a binary ideal solution
Partial pressure of the second component from the measured total
Dalton's law of partial pressures in the vapour
Relative volatility and enrichment of the vapour
Recognising data in a stem that the question does not need
concepts: Molality counts moles of B per kilogram of A while mole fraction counts them against every mole present, so the molality has to be converted before Raoult's law can be used - and the molar mass of A is given for exactly that
Raoult's law uses the LIQUID composition: each component's partial pressure is its own pure vapour pressure scaled by its own mole fraction in the liquid
Once the total pressure is known and one partial pressure has been calculated, the other is simply what is left over - no second application of Raoult's law is needed
Dalton's law governs the vapour: in an ideal gas mixture each component's partial pressure is its mole fraction IN THE VAPOUR times the total, so the vapour composition is just the pressure share
x and y are different numbers for the same vessel at the same moment, and the question is built around a student handing in x
Combining the two laws gives y(i) = x(i)p(i)deg/p(total), so a component less volatile than the mixture as a whole is depleted in the vapour and one more volatile is enriched
Here p(B)deg works out lower than p(A)deg, so B is the less volatile liquid and the vapour ends up poorer in B than the liquid it came from - the enrichment factor is exactly p(B)deg/p(total)
The vapour being richer in the more volatile component is the entire basis of fractional distillation
Three of the five quantities printed in the stem - R, the molar mass of B and the density of liquid B - belong to Q.15 and never enter this answer
formulas: p(A) = x(A) p(A)deg   (Raoult, uses the liquid composition)
p(i) = y(i) p(total)   (Dalton, in the vapour)
combined: y(B) = x(B) p(B)deg / p(total),  y(B)/x(B) = p(B)deg/p(total)

derivedQuantities.richer_phase_in_B: the liquid - B is the less volatile component

methods: Derived from first principles before any published solution was consulted: the molality conversion, Raoult's law for A, the subtraction for B and Dalton's law for the vapour were each fixed independently
Both phases close separately and the pressures reconcile: x(A) + x(B) = 0.80 + 0.20 = 1, y(A) + y(B) = 0.84 + 0.16 = 1, and p(A) + p(B) = 84 + 16 = 100 mm Hg, the total the question states

The answer reproduced by three independent routes: p(B)/p(total) = 0.16 directly; recovering p(B)deg = p(B)/x(B) = 80 mm Hg and using x(B)p(B)deg/p(total) = 0.16; and 1 - x(A)p(A)deg/p(total) = 0.16. The relative-volatility form with alpha = p(A)deg/p(B)deg = 21/16 reproduces y(A) = 0.84 exactly

The direction of the effect predicted before it was computed: p(B)deg < p(A)deg forces the vapour to be poorer in B, and the computed 0.16 < 0.20 agrees - so the result is not an accident of arithmetic

Limiting cases checked, and the simulation reproduces every one of them live: setting p(A)deg equal to the total makes the two liquids equally volatile and returns y(B) = x(B) exactly; setting p(A)deg below the total makes B the more volatile component and returns y(B) > x(B); a vanishing molality returns y(B) towards zero. The model is therefore valid across its whole input range rather than at one point

The basis proved irrelevant rather than assumed: 500 g, 1000 g, 2500 g and 137 g of A all give x(B) = 0.2 and y(B) = 0.16 in exact rational arithmetic, and on the bench the mass of A moves n(A) and n(B) on the gauges while the answer never moves

The three unused quantities confirmed unused: changing the molar mass of B, the density of liquid B and the gas constant all at once leaves the answer at 0.16, which is the structural reason they belong to Q.15
The impossible region handled rather than ignored: a total pressure at or below x(A)p(A)deg would leave B a negative partial pressure, and the bench refuses to run, quoting A's own contribution

The distractors reproduced deliberately, each as a run on the student's own data: handing in x(B) gives 0.20, y(A) gives 0.84, p(B)/p(A) gives 0.1905, slipping p(A)deg into the last step gives 0.21, 1 - x(B) gives 0.80, and p(B)/p(B)deg walks back to 0.20. None is 0.16
Independent numeric script in exact fractions (verify16.py): 28 of 28 checks pass and the answer is 4/25 = 0.16 with no floating-point rounding anywhere

interactivity: Enter the data, run the experiment, watch it produce the answer: an instrument rail you fill in, five stages you watch, and a vapour composition read off the finished run - about thirty-two seconds end to end

The experiment happens inside a dark laboratory chamber that stays dark in either page theme, with glass, depth, glow and molecules under Brownian motion, while the page around it follows the light or dark theme like every other simulation in the library

Nine inputs with a typed box, a slider and a pair of large steppers each - the seven this part uses and three marked as given by the stem but not needed here, because recognising unused data is part of reading a question
Eight live instruments that stay blank until the run establishes them, grouped so the two liquid mole fractions sit beside the two vapour ones - and y(B) stays blank until the very end
Nothing is precomputed: the bench runs on whatever is entered, reaches a different answer for different data, and refuses data it cannot reconcile
The bench refuses a total pressure at or below what A alone contributes and says why, because that would leave B a negative partial pressure - the one physically impossible region of the input space

Stage 01 weighs the solvent into the vessel with a live balance, draws one molecule per mole so n(A) = w(A)/M(A) is counted rather than asserted, and then adds B at the entered molality while the narration says in one line what molality actually means

Stage 02 is a composition analyser: it counts the two populations, builds a stacked 80/20 composition bar from them, writes x(A) and x(B) out - and then puts a warning on screen that x(B) is the LIQUID mole fraction and not the answer, which is the moment the question becomes interesting

Stage 03 seals the vessel and lets both volatile components evaporate, with the vapour's molecule mix following the two partial pressures and an analogue gauge swinging up to the measured total. Raoult's law is then written out and substituted in the student's own numbers, and a stacked pressure bar splits the gauge reading into p(A) and p(B) in front of them

Stage 04 is the heart of it: twenty-five molecules drawn for each phase, side by side, in the proportion that phase actually has. Five are B on the liquid side and four on the vapour side, and the student can simply count them before any division is done
Dalton's law is stated as the reason the vapour composition is a pressure share, and the final division is set up with the answer withheld

The reveal darkens the laboratory for about a second, then flashes, sprays the answer across the chamber in graffiti lettering with a burst of confetti and chemical glyphs, blinks the header answer box once and unlocks the derivation
A permanent split comparison below the bench keeps both phases side by side with their molecule counts, under a caption reading liquid composition then vapour pressures then vapour composition

A y-against-x diagram drawn from the entered data, with the y = x diagonal for reference so the gap is visible everywhere, and a slider to explore any composition - reporting the vapour composition there, the total pressure there, and which phase is the richer in B
A second view drawing the bubble and dew curves together, where the horizontal gap between them at the measured pressure is exactly x(B) - y(B); it stays locked until the run has measured p(B)deg
A record of the run that fills in quantity by quantity, and a trial log of every completed run - with an insight card naming what can and cannot move the answer
Six cards on the mistakes this question really produces, each re-running the model with one wrong assumption on the student's own numbers: 0.20, 0.84, 0.1905, 0.21, 0.80 and 0.20

CLASSROOM MODE for a projector: the rail and the surrounding sections are hidden, the stage and the narration scale up, and a NEXT STEP button walks the class through molality, x(A), x(B), p(A), p(B), y(B) and the answer one press at a time with the clock paused in between

A full-screen button for the bench, playback controls - pause, resume, replay, 0.5x / 1x / 2x - and a change-the-data button that returns to the rail with the entries kept; every box stays editable during the run and every instrument follows it
Step-by-step solution with an independent verification log, gated until the answer is revealed
Four concept cards - molality is not mole fraction, Raoult's law, Dalton's law, and the connection y = x p(deg)/p(T) - that animate in when the answer lands and fill their numbers in only then
